claims.claim: The Wrights' 1901 wind tunnel was six feet long with a sixteen-inch-square test section.
claims.episode_span: They built a wind tunnel sixteen inches square and six feet long, powered by a small fan
claims.supporting_quote: It was six feet long, sixteen inches wide, and 16 inches deep

claims.claim: The Wrights tested on the order of two hundred model wing shapes in their wind tunnel (Smithsonian: 'as many as 200 different model wing shapes', with formal data recorded on nearly 50).
claims.episode_span: tested more than two hundred airfoil shapes, recording lift and drag on a homemade balance
claims.source_title: Researching the Wright Way | National Air and Space Museum
claims.supporting_quote: Wilbur and Orville conducted preliminary tests on as many as 200 different model wing shapes as they perfected the operation of their wind tunnel

claims.claim: On 17 December 1903 the best flight of the day, with Wilbur at the controls, covered 852 feet in 59 seconds.
claims.episode_span: On 17 December 1903 the 1903 Flyer, powered by a twelve-horsepower engine the brothers cast themselves, flew 852 feet in 59 seconds
claims.source_title: 1903 Wright Flyer | National Air and Space Museum
claims.supporting_quote: The best flight of the day, with Wilbur at the controls, covered 255.6 m (852 ft) in 59 seconds

claims.claim: The 1903 Flyer's engine was a small twelve-horsepower gasoline engine the Wrights built with their shop mechanic Charles Taylor.
claims.episode_span: powered by a twelve-horsepower engine the brothers cast themselves
claims.source_title: 1903 Wright Flyer | National Air and Space Museum
claims.supporting_quote: With the assistance of their bicycle shop mechanic, Charles Taylor, the Wrights built a small, twelve-horsepower gasoline engine

claims.claim: Langley's full-scale Aerodrome was funded with $50,000 in War Department grants (plus Smithsonian funds), supporting the digest's 'more than fifty thousand dollars in federal and private money'.
claims.episode_span: Samuel Langley at the Smithsonian had received more than fifty thousand dollars in federal and private money by 1903
claims.supporting_quote: made $50,000 in grants to the Smithsonian for construction of a full-scale man-carrying version

claims.claim: Langley's Aerodrome fell into the Potomac River on both 1903 launch attempts (October 7 and December 8).
claims.episode_span: The same year Langley’s heavily funded Aerodrome plunged into the Potomac twice.
claims.supporting_quote: On the first flight attempt, October 7, 1903, the craft failed to fly and dropped into the Potomac River immediately after launch. On the second attempt, December 8, the craft collapsed after launch and again fell into the river
